source_text: Οὐχ ὁ τὸν πόδα προσπταίσας ἐπιζητεῖ τὸ τοῦ ὀφθαλ μοῦ ἴαμα· ἀλλ' ὁ τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν κεκακωμένον ἔχων ζητεῖ τὸ οἰκεῖον τῷ πάθει βοήθημα. Οὐκοῦν ἕκαστος ἐκ τῆς Γραφῆς λαμβανέτω τὰ συγγενῆ τῷ ἰδίῳ πάθει. Θυμώδης εἶ; κατάστειλον τὸν θυμόν. «Θυμώδης γὰρ, φησὶν, ἀνὴρ οὐκ εὐσχήμων.» Μάθε παρὰ τῆς Γραφῆς. Κάτοπτρον γενέσθω τοῦ προσώπου τοῦ σοῦ ἡ Γραφή. Ἐκεῖ μάθε. Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀσεβὴς λογισμὸς σκοτώσας οὐκ ἐᾷ λογίσασθαί σε ἡλίκον ἁμάρτημά ἐστιν ὁ θυμὸς, ἡ Γραφή σοι λέγει· «Οὐκ εὐσχήμων ἀνὴρ θυμώδης.» Πῶς ἀσχημονεῖ ὁ θυμώδης; Ἀποτίθεται τὸ σχῆμα τὸ ἀνθρώ πινον, θηρίου σχῆμα μεταλαμβάνει. Ἐννόησον τὸν θυμούμενον. Ἐπέζεσεν αὐτῷ ὁ θυμὸς, καὶ οἱ ὀφθαλ μοὶ ὑπηλλάγησαν· οὐκ εἰσὶν οἱ αὐτοὶ ὀφθαλμοὶ, πῦρ βλέπει, ἀνέδραμεν αὐτῷ τὸ αἷμα, περιέζεσε τὴν καρδίαν, περιέδραμε τοὺς χιτῶνας τῶν ὀφθαλ μῶν, ἐγένετο ὕφαιμος ἐκχωρῶν τῷ πάθει, ἠλλοίωσεν αὐτοῦ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς. «Ἀνὴρ θυμώδης οὐκ εὐσχήμων.» Ἐὰν ἴδῃς τὸν θυμούμενον τοὺς ὀδόντας παραθήγοντα, ἐνθυμήθητι, ὅτι συῒ ἔοικεν ὁ τοιοῦτος, τὸν ἔνδοθεν θυμὸν διὰ τῆς τῶν ὀδόντων παρατρίψεως ὑπεκφαίνων. Ἐὰν ἴδῃς τὸν θυμούμενον ἀφρίζοντα· ἐὰν ἴδῃς ἄσημα φθεγγόμενον ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ· ἐὰν ἴδῃς τὸν θυμούμενον πατρὸς μὲν ἐπιλανθανόμενον παι δὸς δὲ ἀγνοοῦντα σῶμα, διὰ πάντων ἀφειδῶς χω ροῦντα, ἵνα πληροφορήσῃ αὐτοῦ τὴν ὁρμὴν, βλέπεις τὴν ἀσχημοσύνην τοῦ πράγματος. Ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ κακῷ σεαυτὸν θεράπευσον, ἵνα μὴ τὴν ἐκείνου ἀσχημοσύνην καὶ αὐτὸς λάβῃς. «Ἀνὴρ θυμώδης οὐκ εὐσχήμων.» Καὶ, «Ἀνδρὶ θυμώδει μὴ συναυλίζου.» Κακὸν πρᾶγμα κυνὶ συνδεδέσθαι, καὶ διηνεκοῦς ὑλακῆς ἀπολαύειν. Ἀνὴρ θυμώδης οὐκ εὐσχήμων.» Φεῦγε τὰς μετ' αὐτοῦ διατριβάς· ἀνάγκη γάρ σε μαθεῖν τι τῶν ἐκείνου ὁδῶν. Εἶπέ τι ὑβριστικὸν, ἐκίνησε καὶ τὸν ἐν σοὶ θυμόν. Ὥσπερ κυνὸς ὑλακὴ προκαλεῖται ἑτέρου κυνὸς θόρυβον, καὶ τὸν ἐν σοὶ θυμὸν τέως κοιμώμενον καὶ ἡσυχάζοντα ἡ ἐκείνου φωνὴ διήγειρε, καὶ γεγόνατε ἀλλήλοις ἀνθυλακτοῦντες, εἶτα ἀντικαταστάντες ἀλλήλοις, ὥσπερ σφενδόνας ἀφίετε τῶν ῥημάτων τῆς ἀσχημοσύνης. Εἶπέ τι ὑβριστικὸν ἐκεῖνος, ἀντέδωκας σὺ μείζονι ὑπερβολῇ, τὸν προλαβόντα μιμούμενος. Λαβὼν ἐκεῖνος τὴν ἐκ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ ὑβριστικοῦ ἀντίδοσιν, οὐκ ἔστι τῆς ὁρμῆς, ἀλλ' ἐστράφη καὶ ἐκορύφωσε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἁμαρτίαν. Μείζων ἐβουλήθη γενέσθαι ἐκ τοῦ εἰπεῖν τι χαλεπώτερον. Σὺ δὲ, δεξάμενος πάλιν, ὑπερυψώθης· καὶ γέγονε κακῶν φιλονεικία. Ὁ δὲ ἐν κακῶν ἁμίλλαις νικῶν, οὗτος ἀθλιώτερός ἐστιν. «Ἀνὴρ θυμώδης οὐκ εὐσχήμων·» καὶ, «Ἀνδρὶ θυμώδει μὴ συναυλίζου.» «Μηδὲ συνδείπνει ἀνδρὶ βασκάνῳ.» Ἕτερον πάθος ἐμπολιτευόμενον τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ ἀεὶ προσπεφυκὸς ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἡμῶν, καὶ μᾶλλον δαπανῶν τὴν καρδίαν ἢ ὁ ἰὸς τὸν σίδηρον, ἡ βασκανία ἐστὶν, ἐν ᾗ πολλὰ μέν ἐστι κακὰ, ἓν δὲ χρήσι μον, ὅτι κακόν ἐστιν αὐτῷ τῷ κεκτημένῳ. Ὁ γὰρ βάσκανος αὐτὸν μὲν τὸν βασκαινόμενον ὀλίγα βλάπτει, ἑαυτὸν δὲ δαπανᾷ τῇ λύπῃ καὶ τῷ στεναγμῷ ἐπὶ τῇ εὐημερίᾳ τοῦ πλησίον· καὶ τὴν μὲν χώραν τοῦ γείτονος οὐκ ἠλάττωσεν, ἑαυτὸν δὲ κατεδαπάνησε τῇ βασκανίᾳ. «Μὴ μέταιρε ὅρια αἰώνια. Εἰς δὲ κτῆμα ὀρφανῶν μὴ εἰσέλθῃς.» Μὴ εἰσέλθῃς εἰς τὸ τῶν ὀρφανῶν κτῆμα, ἵνα εἰσέλθῃς εἰς τὸ σὸν κτῆμα.
thought_title: Anger disfigures and envy eats its owner
orientation: The preacher continues giving matching scriptural cures for each passion, now treating anger at length and then turning to envy.
pass_a_gloss: The one who stumbled with his foot does not seek the cure for the eye; but the one who has his eye injured seeks the help that belongs to his suffering. Therefore let each take from Scripture the things kindred to his own passion. Are you quick-tempered? Restrain your anger. For, it says, a quick-tempered man is not decent. Learn from Scripture. Let Scripture become a mirror of your face. Learn there. Since your impious reasoning, having darkened you, does not allow you to reckon how great a sin anger is, Scripture says to you: A quick-tempered man is not decent. How does the quick-tempered man act unseemly? He lays aside the human form, he takes on the form of a wild beast. Consider the man in anger. His anger boiled up in him, and his eyes were altered; they are not the same eyes, he looks fire, his blood ran up in him, it boiled around his heart, it ran around the coats of his eyes, he became bloodshot, yielding to his passion, it changed his eyes. A quick-tempered man is not decent. If you see the man in anger grinding his teeth, consider that such a one is like a pig, displaying his inward anger through the grinding of his teeth. If you see the man in anger foaming; if you see him uttering indistinct sounds in his heart; if you see the man in anger forgetting his father and not recognizing the body of his child, rushing without mercy through all things, so that he may fulfill his impulse, you see the unseemliness of the matter. Heal yourself by another's evil, so that you yourself may not also take his unseemliness. A quick-tempered man is not decent. And, Do not lodge with a quick-tempered man. It is an evil thing to be tied to a dog and to enjoy its continual barking. A quick-tempered man is not decent. Flee spending time with him; for you must learn something of his ways. He said something insulting, and he stirred up also the anger in you. As the barking of a dog provokes the clamor of another dog, so his voice woke up the anger in you, which until now was sleeping and quiet, and you became barking back at each other, then standing against each other, as slings you hurl the words of unseemliness. That one said something insulting, you paid it back with greater excess, imitating the one who began. That one, receiving the return from your insulting speech, does not hold back his impulse, but he turned and crowned his own sin. He wished to become greater by saying something harsher. And you, receiving it again, were lifted up; and a quarrel of evils came to be. But the one who wins in contests of evils, this one is more wretched. A quick-tempered man is not decent; and, Do not lodge with a quick-tempered man. And, Do not eat with an envious man. There is another passion living among the life of human beings, and always clinging to our souls, and consuming the heart more than rust consumes iron: it is envy, in which there are many evils, but one useful thing, that it is evil to the one who possesses it. For the envious man harms the one who is envied little, but he consumes himself with grief and groaning at the prosperity of his neighbor; and he did not lessen the land of his neighbor, but he consumed himself with envy. Do not move ancient boundaries. And do not enter into the property of orphans. Do not enter into the property of orphans, so that you may enter into your own property.

pass_b_english: A man who stubs his foot does not look for a cure for the eye. A man with an injured eye seeks the help that fits his own hurt. So let each of you take from Scripture what matches your own passion. Are you quick-tempered? Restrain your anger. For Scripture says, "A quick-tempered man is not decent" (Proverbs 11:25). Learn from Scripture. Let Scripture become a mirror for your face. Look and learn there.

An ungodly line of thought darkens you. It keeps you from reckoning how great a sin anger is. So Scripture tells you, "A quick-tempered man is not decent" (Proverbs 11:25). How does a quick-tempered man show his indecency? He lays aside the human form. He takes on the form of a wild beast. Picture someone seized by anger. Anger boils up in him. His eyes change. They are no longer the same eyes. He looks fire. The blood rushes up in him. It seethes around his heart. It courses around the coverings of his eyes. He grows bloodshot as he surrenders to his passion. It alters his eyes. Scripture says, "A quick-tempered man is not decent" (Proverbs 11:25).

If you see someone in anger grinding his teeth, remember this. Such a person is like a pig. He shows the anger inside by grinding his teeth. If you see someone in anger foaming at the mouth, if you hear him uttering broken sounds from his heart, if you see him forgetting his father and failing to recognize the body of his own child, rushing without mercy through every obstacle to satisfy his impulse, you see the indecency of the thing. Heal yourself by another man's evil, so you do not take his indecency upon yourself. Scripture says, "A quick-tempered man is not decent" (Proverbs 11:25), and, "Do not lodge with a quick-tempered man" (Proverbs 22:24).

It is a wretched thing to be tied to a dog and to endure its endless barking. Scripture says, "A quick-tempered man is not decent" (Proverbs 11:25). Flee his company. You will have to learn some of his ways. He speaks an insult. It stirs the anger in you. One dog's bark rouses another dog's clamor. In the same way his voice wakes the anger in you, though it was sleeping and quiet for a time. Then you bark back at each other. Then you set yourselves against each other. Like slings you hurl indecent words. He speaks an insult. You pay him back with still greater excess, copying the man who began it. He receives that return for his insulting speech. He does not check his impulse. He turns and crowns his own sin. He means to come out greater by saying something harsher. You take it in turn and rise still higher. A rivalry of evils results. The winner in a contest of evils is the more wretched. Scripture says, "A quick-tempered man is not decent" (Proverbs 11:25), and, "Do not lodge with a quick-tempered man" (Proverbs 22:24), and, "Do not dine with an envious man" (Proverbs 23:6).

There is another passion at work in human life. It clings to our souls always. It eats the heart more than rust eats iron. It is envy. It holds many evils, and one useful point. It is an evil to the man who holds it. The envious man harms the man he envies only a little. He consumes himself with grief and groaning at his neighbor's prosperity. He has not made his neighbor's land smaller. He has consumed himself by envy. Scripture says, "Do not move ancient boundaries, and do not enter the property of orphans" (Proverbs 23:10). Do not enter the property of orphans, so you may enter into your own property.

last_rejected.why: Those words are the extra Septuagint clause at Proverbs 11:25. A standard English Bible has a different sentence there.
last_rejected.fix: Cite it as Proverbs 11:25 LXX wherever this saying is quoted.
last_rejected.ruling: Θυμώδης ἀνὴρ οὐκ εὐσχήμων is the Septuagint clause at Proverbs 11:25. The other citations (22:24, 23:6, 23:10) also follow Septuagint numbering, so the reference is consistent.

last_rejected.why: The Greek means he sees fire. The English is not a readable equivalent and shifts sight to appearance.
last_rejected.ruling: πῦρ βλέπει means he glares fire, as the eyes change. 'Looks fire' is stiff but keeps the sense; the meaning is not lost or misleading. Mere style.
